fields.description: Five questions covering the same topics on every attempt. Pass with at least three correct.

fields.title: Crops Had Different Uses
fields.content:
Agriculture supplied food, materials and products for sale. A household could use part of a harvest at home and exchange another part. A crop grown for sale is often called a cash crop. The name describes its purpose in a transaction, not a promise that the grower became wealthy. Food crops could also be sold. We should ask how a harvest was used instead of dividing all plants into two fixed groups.

Imagine a fictional harvest card showing rice kept for meals and rice offered for sale. The same crop serves different needs. Selling part of it may bring money, but a sales total alone does not tell us what the household spent on seed, tools or transport. Nor does it show the food left at home. This model is a teaching example, not a surviving farm account. Look for the use, the work and the resources involved before explaining a household economy.

fields.title: Rules Could Change Economic Choices
fields.content:
An economic policy can affect what people produce, who they may sell to and what resources an authority receives. A policy has an aim, but its aim is not proof of its actual results. To investigate one, connect the rule with records of what people did and how it affected them. Different groups might gain or lose in different ways.

Try a fictional market comparison. In Card A, growers can choose among several buyers. In Card B, a rule requires delivery to one authorized buyer. Even without inventing a price, you can see a difference in choice. The cards are models, not descriptions of all markets during Spanish rule. For an actual policy, ask which product, place and period it covered. A rule about one crop does not establish control over every product everywhere.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

fields.title: A Named Policy: The Tobacco Monopoly
fields.content:
The tobacco monopoly is a named example of colonial economic control. The NHCP historical marker dates its formal establishment to March 1782 under Governor Jose Basco y Vargas. It also records abolition in 1882. These dates identify this policy period; they do not mean tobacco farming itself began and ended on those dates.

Wolters describes compulsory cultivation in designated districts and government purchase of the crop at an officially determined price. This restricted growers choices about production and sale. Do not turn designated districts into a claim about every farm in all the islands. Our diagram shows a simplified relationship between growers and the government, not a map of every covered district. We study the crop to understand colonial power. This lesson does not encourage growing, handling or using tobacco.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

fields.title: Compare Income, Costs and Choices
fields.content:
A policy could bring revenue to the government while placing burdens on growers. Revenue means income received; it is not the same as profit after expenses. To explain effects on a household, ask about work, materials, the price received and available choices. A large government collection alone cannot prove that all growers benefited.

Use a fictional account model with no historical price claim. A grower receives eight tokens from a sale and has five tokens of costs. Three remain after those listed costs. Another card showing only eight received leaves the costs unknown. The tokens are not pesos, crop quotas or points earned by controlling other people. In an actual case, look for dated accounts and consider whether some costs or unpaid work are missing. A simple total cannot tell us every experience.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

fields.title: Follow a Policy Through Time
fields.content:
Policies could change or end. Abolition of the tobacco monopoly ended that particular government arrangement; it did not mean that all farming, trade or taxation stopped. A date tells us when an institutional change is recorded. To explain what followed, we need evidence about later activity as well as the earlier rule.

Imagine a fictional exhibit with three cards: an old monopoly instruction, a later abolition notice and a farm account after the change. The instruction helps explain a required arrangement. The notice records an institutional ending. The farm account helps investigate later production and exchange. Do not ask one card to answer every question. Keep an official aim separate from implementation, and compare how particular people experienced the transition instead of assuming everyone gained equally.

Open the three evidence clues, then choose the explanation they support. Use Explain if you want help. Review this lesson before targeted practice when the topic needs another look.

fields.title: Prepare Your Agriculture Policy Report
fields.content:
Review five ideas. Harvests could serve household and market needs. Economic rules could affect choices about production and buyers. The tobacco monopoly is a named, dated example of government control. Revenue and income remaining after costs are different questions. A policy ending does not mean all economic activity ended.

Prepare a fictional museum report for another Grade 5 learner. Name a policy, identify a supporting clue and explain its scope. Compare a government aim with evidence about growers experiences. If you use the eight-minus-five token model, label it as a teaching model rather than a historical crop price. Do not present every community as identical or treat every recorded receipt as profit.

The main quiz has five questions; three correct passes. Review linked learning content before practice and a retry if needed. Completing this mission earns its configured reward once. It does not finish Chapter 9: Missions 4-5 and the chapter challenge are still being prepared.
